items.exact_text: Universam significabat ecclesiam, quae in hoc seculo diversis tentationibus, velut imbribus, fluminibus, tempestatibusque quatitur, et non cadit; quoniam fundata est supra Petram; unde et Petrus nomen accepit. Non enim a Petro Petra, sed Petrus a Petra; sicut non Christus a Christiano, sed Christianus a Christo vocatur. Ideo quippe ait Dominus, 'Super hanc Petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam', quia dixerat Petrus, 'Tu es Christus filius Dei vivi'. 'Super hanc ergo' (inquit) 'Petram quam confessus es, aedificabo ecclesiam meam'. Petra enim erat Christus, super quod fundamentum etiam ipse aedificatus est Petrus. Fundamentum quippe aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Jesus Christus
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: It signified the universal church, which in this age is shaken by various temptations, like rains, rivers, and storms, and does not fall; because it is founded upon a Rock; from which Peter also received his name. For the Rock is not called from Peter, but Peter from the Rock; just as Christ is not called from Christian, but Christian from Christ. Therefore, the Lord says, 'Upon this Rock I will build my church', because Peter had said, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God'. 'Upon this Rock, therefore' (He says) 'which you have confessed, I will build my church'. For the Rock was Christ, upon which foundation Peter himself was also built. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. (Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractate 124)

items.exact_text: Filius Dei existens semper apud Patrem, et homo factus, longam hominum expositionem in seipso recapitulavit; in compendio nobis salutem praestans, ut quod perdideramus in Adam, id est, secundum imaginem et similitudinem esse Dei, hoc in Christo Jesus reciperemus. Quia enim non erat ppossibile, eum hominem, qui semel victus fuerat et elisus per inobedientiam, replasmare et obtinere brabium (βρᾶβεῖον) victoriae; iterum autem impossibile erat ut salutem perciperet, qui sub peccato ceciderat. Utraque operatus est filius Verbum Dei existens, a Patre descendens et incarnatus, et usque ad mortem descendens, et dispensationem consummans salutis nostrae
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: The Son of God, always existing with the Father, and made man, recapitulated in Himself the long line of human beings; furnishing us with salvation in a compendium, so that what we had lost in Adam, that is, to be according to the image and likeness of God, this we should recover in Christ Jesus. For because it was not possible that the man who had once been conquered and destroyed through disobedience should be reformed and obtain the prize of victory; and again it was impossible that he should receive salvation who had fallen under sin. The Son, being the Word of God, descending from the Father and incarnate, and descending even to death, and consummating the dispensation of our salvation, accomplished both. (Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses, Book 3, Chapter 18)

items.exact_text: Non in semetipso recapitulasset haec Dominus, nisi ipse caro et sanguis secundum principalem plasmationem factus fuisset; salvans in semetipso in fine illud quod perierat in principio in Adam. Si autem ob aliam quandam dispositionem Dominus incarnatus est, et ex altera substantia carnem attulit, non ergo in semetipso recapitulatus est hominem, adhuc etiam nec aro quidem dici potest... Habuit ergo et ipse carnem et sanguinem, non alteram quindam, sed ipsam principalem Patris plasmationem in se recapitulans, exquirens id quod perierat
items.translation_text: Modern Translation: The Lord would not have recapitulated these things in Himself, unless He Himself had been made flesh and blood according to the original creation; saving in Himself at the end that which had perished at the beginning in Adam. But if the Lord was incarnate for some other dispensation, and brought flesh from another substance, He has not then recapitulated humanity in Himself, nor indeed can He be called flesh... He therefore had Himself both flesh and blood, not of another kind, but recapitulating in Himself the very original creation of the Father, seeking out that which had perished. (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book 5, Chapter 14)

items.exact_text: Κατοπτρίζω does not admit of the signification here ascribed to it by Dr Owen. It denotes looking into a mirror, not through a telescope: "Beholding the glory of the Lord as reflected and radiant in the Gospel." See Dr Robinson's Lexicon. Another view is taken of the passage, by which a tacit antithesis is instituted between κάτοπτρον and ἐικών: "Dominus nos κατοπτρίζει, splendorem faciei suae in corda nostram, tanquam in specula immittens: nos illum splendorem suscipimus et referimus. Elegans antitheton ad ἐντετυπωμένη, insculpta. Nam quae insculpuntur fiunt paullatim: quae in speculo repraesentantur, fiunt celerrime." Bengelii Gnomon in locum. Owen himself gives a correct explanation of the passage in his work on the Mortification of Sin, chap. 12. Ed.
items.modern_reference:
Modern Citation: Johann Albrecht Bengel, Gnomon Novi Testamenti, on 2 Corinthians 3:18; Edward Robinson, A Greek and English Lexicon of the New Testament, s.v. κατοπτρίζω.
Translation: Κατοπτρίζω means “to behold as in a mirror” or “to reflect as a mirror,” not “to look through a telescope.” Bengel's Latin means: “The Lord mirrors himself to us, sending the splendor of his face into our hearts as into mirrors; we receive and reflect that splendor. This is an elegant contrast with ‘engraved’ or ‘inscribed’; for things engraved are made gradually, but things represented in a mirror are made very quickly.”

items.exact_text: Born at Germanicia, in the north or Syria ordained a presbyter at Antioch appointed patriarch of Constantinople A.D.428 objected to the epithet Θεοτόκος, as applied to the Virgin Mary, because "that God should be born of a human being is impossible" charged in consequence with maintaining that Christ was a mere man held in reality the distinct separation of the divine and human natures of Christ, insisting on a connection between them by συνάφεια (junction), or ἐνοίκησις (indwelling), in opposition to ἕνωσις (union) deposed by the Third General Council of Ephesus, A.D.431, and died probably before A.D. 450. ED. 636
items.modern_reference: Modern Citation: Nestorius of Constantinople, controversy over the title Θεοτόκος (“God-bearer”), condemned at the Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431); see Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History, Book 7, Chapters 29–34 [NPNF2, 2:169–178; PG 67.793–824], and the conciliar acts of Ephesus.

Modern Citation: Nestorius of Constantinople, controversy over the title Θεοτόκος (“God-bearer”), condemned at the Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431); see Socrates Scholasticus, Ecclesiastical History, Book 7, Chapters 29–34 [NPNF2, 2:169–178; PG 67.793–824], and the conciliar acts of Ephesus.
Translation Summary: The Greek terms are technical Christological vocabulary: Θεοτόκος means “God-bearer” or “Mother of God”; συνάφεια means “conjunction” or “association”; ἐνοίκησις means “indwelling”; and ἕνωσις means “union.” The note explains that Nestorius preferred language of conjunction or indwelling between Christ's two natures rather than the orthodox language of true personal union.
